blocks.text: That ants are winged, and lose their wings only after the mating performed in the air, the Talmud seems not to have known, and only Aristotle (l. c. 4, 1, 3) speaks of winged and wingless ants, likewise Voigt (l. c. 4. p. 292); the Talmud therefore speaks only of the latter. — Strange are the words of Maimuni (Hil. Maachaloth asuroth c. 2. §. 24): נמלה הפרחת הגדלה במים, which Abraham b. David already rejects as false, for the ant is not an aquatic insect; Maimuni, on the other hand, expresses himself correctly in the introduction to the Order Seraïm (Ed. Sulzbach fol. 89, d): קצת הנמלים בכנפים ומהם בלי כנפים, “some ants are winged, others wingless.”

The Midrash (Jalkut Schim, 2. part fol. 134b) contains several natural-historical statements about the ant, which we report here. The anthill has three chambers; the store is kept in the middle one, because in the upper one it could be spoiled by the rain and in the lower one by dirt. — The ant gathers wheat, barley and lentils. — It lives only six months. — It consumes only one and a half grains of wheat. The other statements are fabulous, and therefore we leave them unmentioned.

In Arabic the word is written سمسمة [simsima], in Syriac ܫܘܡܫܡܢܐ [שומשמנא], in Chaldaic in the three forms given above; however, the Arabic word means only the red ant; the black or small ant is called: نملة [namla].

It is, moreover, still very questionable whether a stone is meant here and not rather a mountain; Jonathan (on 4. B. M. 21, 35) has טורא, which means only mountain; in the Talmud passage (54a and b), to be sure, טורא is identified with אבן.
The cabbage caterpillar is called in Greek: Κραμβίς [krambis],
Thus Rashi has טיינשא for טינשא, cf. §. 443.
